strengths: This paper studies an important problem of generalization to unseen symbols in transformer architectures.
Much of the contribution is formalizing a set of symbolic reasoning tasks which can be analyzed in different architectures.

The authors give a theoretical analysis that suggests implementation tweaks (adding the identity matrices) which improve performance on real-valued template tasks and preserve good performance on natural language modeling.
They also give an important separation result between multi-layer perceptrons and transformer architectures and explain why the transformers can learn the real-valued regression tasks at large width.
Lastly they observe that large embedding dimension can be harmful in transformers on copy tasks.
I appreciate the effort the authors took in performing experiments (several in the Appendix) to evaluate their theoretical claims, which are often lacking in theory papers.
I find the targeted problem valuable and exciting.
The tasks established earlier in the paper are very well described and the results are accordingly insightful.
The authors conduct a thorough theoretical analysis with practical insights suggesting changes to the transformer architecture.
The work studies if transformers are capable of symbol binding, which is a very important question and of broad interest to the community.
The paper presents a diverse set of results, but makes them easy to understand to a broader audience.
The template tasks are elegant and easy to understand, grounding the problem in a concrete scenario that can be studied.
The authors present concrete insights for real labels and symbolic labels and identify different sample complexity behaviors for both scenarios.
The work identifies important factors like data diversity or transformer embedding size that change the convergence behavior.

The authors use their theory to develop practical insights for developing transformer architectures, showing experiments on a synthetic dataset and on Wikitext to validate their proposed modification.
The author provides a theoretical formulation of variable-binding tasks called template tasks.
Proofs are provided for the capability and limitations of a simplified transformer architecture on two instantiations of template tasks.
Extensive empirical experiments are conducted on the template task framework.

The paper presents a formal analysis of OOD symbolic reasoning in both transformers and MLPs, finding that transformers, but not MLPs, are theoretically capable of a form of abstract symbolic reasoning, given sufficient training data diversity, providing interesting insights into the source of reasoning capabilities in LLMs and contrasting with the view that capabilities are due exclusively to scale.

The analysis yields a novel modification to transformers that further improves their abstract reasoning capabilities, improving sample efficiency on one class of tasks, and enabling generalization on another.
The proposed modification also yields improved performance in a pretrained LLM (GPT-2) on a realistic task (wikitext).
weaknesses: The main result for transformers relies on operating the model in the kernel regime.
It is unclear at the moment if any of the results would change (1) at finite width or (2) in the feature learning regime.
The theoretical analysis hinges on the Neural Network Gaussian Process (NNGP) kernel, which assumes infinite width.
The practical implications of this assumption need further exploration, as real-world networks operate at finite widths where the kernel approximation may not hold.
The paper does not fully explore the transition from the kernel regime to the feature learning regime, where the network's internal weights are updated.

This transition could potentially alter the observed generalization behavior, and it is not clear if the block diagonal structure of the kernel would still be preserved when the network learns its own features.

The proposed theory bounds the generalization error in terms of the data diversity metric, which does not have an obvious scaling with samples n, making it hard to reason about the number of samples needed to attain good generalization.
The data diversity metric, while useful for characterizing the input space, lacks a clear connection to the number of training samples needed to achieve a desired level of generalization.
It would be beneficial to have a more explicit relationship between the data diversity metric and the number of training samples required for the model to generalize effectively.

The authors are over-claiming their results; the simplified architecture studied (self-attention + MLP) is not justified to be labeled a Transformer, lacking residual connections, layer normalization, and multi-head attention, which significantly alter behavior, leading to potentially incorrect takeaway that Transformers broadly cannot perform variable binding tasks; also results focus on single-pass inference, ignoring in-context learning or chain-of-thought.

Lack of experimental details: unclear whether experiments use simplified architecture or actual Transformer with residual connections, layer normalization, multi-head attention; specific hyperparameters, optimization algorithms, training procedures not clearly detailed (learning rate, batch size, epochs).
Relation with prior theoretical works on inductive biases of self-attention: need thorough discussion of Edelman et al. [1] and empirical works like Davies et al. [2], comparing findings.
Discussion with systematic generalization: need discussion of relation to the SCAN benchmark and other systematic generalization works [3] and how current findings relate.

The theory for the transformers seems to rely on training only the final layer of the transformer, leaving unclear whether other architectures can also do symbol binding and which aspects (attention, MLP, invariance properties) are important.

A limitation of most theory that uses the PAC framework is that it often has vacuous bounds; while the paper derives asymptotic trends, it is unclear if they will be predictive of practical behavior, raising doubt whether this probabilistic framework is the right tool for analysis.

The assumption of a simplified depth-1 transformer architecture without residual connections and layer normalization limits the applicability of the main theoretical conclusions to more practical settings.
All empirical results use a vanilla depth-2 transformer without modification, making it hard to draw direct parallels to justify the practical implications of the theoretical results.

The theoretical analysis focuses on a single self-attention layer followed by an MLP, neglecting the impact of multi-layered architectures and the stabilizing effects of residual connections and layer normalization.
The absence of residual connections and layer normalization raises questions about the generalizability of the proven claims to real-world transformer models.
Empirical results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed attention modification but do not directly validate the theoretical findings due to architectural discrepancies.

The abstract and introduction refer to 'transformer large language models' but experiments in Figures 1 and 2 are on transformers trained from scratch, not on LLMs; it would be clearer to refer to transformers rather than LLMs in the abstract and introduction.

It would be helpful if an intuitive characterization of the proposed modifications ($aI$ and $bI$) could be provided earlier in the paper, along with some sense of why this modification helps; currently the paper dives directly into the mathematical formulation without a clear conceptual picture.

Do the wikitext experiments involve OOD generalization in any sense? If not, this may explain smaller relative improvement; the lack of explicit OOD generalization makes it difficult to directly compare the impact of the modifications on abstract reasoning capabilities.
Clarification is needed on the distinction between GPT-2 and 'GPT-2 pretrained'—whether Figure 4 reflects pretrained GPT-2 fine‑tuned on wikitext or both models are trained from scratch.
The legend is cut off in figure 3a; in general the figure text is very small and difficult to read.
